arXiv:2509.01685v1 [stat.ML] 01 Sep 2025

Preconditioned Regularized Wasserstein Proximal Sampling Methods

Hong Ye Tan ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, University of California, Los Angeles, 90095 (). Email: hyt35,sjo@math.ucla.edu    Stanley Osher22footnotemark: 2    Wuchen Li ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC 29208 () Email: wuchen@mailbox.sc.edu
Abstract

We consider sampling from a Gibbs distribution by evolving finitely many particles. We propose a preconditioned version of a recently proposed noise-free sampling method, governed by approximating the score function with the numerically tractable score of a regularized Wasserstein proximal operator. This is derived by a Cole–Hopf transformation on coupled anisotropic heat equations, yielding a kernel formulation for the preconditioned regularized Wasserstein proximal. The diffusion component of the proposed method is also interpreted as a modified self-attention block, as in transformer architectures. For quadratic potentials, we provide a discrete-time non-asymptotic convergence analysis and explicitly characterize the bias, which is dependent on regularization and independent of step-size. Experiments demonstrate acceleration and particle-level stability on various log-concave and non-log-concave toy examples to Bayesian total-variation regularized image deconvolution, and competitive/better performance on non-convex Bayesian neural network training when utilizing variable preconditioning matrices.

keywords
Sampling, Cole-Hopf, regularized Wasserstein proximal, preconditioning, kernel formula, score approximation, MCMC

1 Introduction

We are interested in sampling from a Gibbs distribution

π⁡(x)∝exp⁡(−β​V​(x)),\pi(x)\propto\exp(-\beta V(x)), (1)

where V:ℝd→ℝV:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is some 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} potential, and β>0\beta>0 is a constant. Such problems arise frequently in data science, such as uncertainty quantification in imaging [28], Bayesian statistical inference [12], inverse problems [42], and computational physics [25]. Methods for sampling have also been connected to recent machine learning methods, such as simulating stochastic differential equations (SDEs) for diffusion models [40], unsupervised learning [44], and Bayesian neural networks [31].

Current popular sampling methods to solve this are Monte Carlo Markov chain (MCMC) methods, which bypass the usual difficulty arising from the intractability of the normalizing constant ∫ℝdexp⁡(−β​V​(x))​dx\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\exp(-\beta V(x))\differential{x}. There is a wide variety of Monte Carlo methods each with different convergence rates and conditions on the potential VV. Notable examples include the unadjusted Langevin algorithm and the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm [36, 10], with recent algorithms considering proximal operators and Moreau–Yosida envelopes [11], subgradients [16], and annealed Moreau regularization [15]. The theoretical core of MCMC is to construct a Markov chain with some invariant distribution π^\hat{\pi} that approximates the target distribution π\pi.

To construct such a Markov chain, a crucial theoretical component is exponential or geometric ergodicity of the chain. In typical Langevin methods, this is given by the Wiener diffusion term, which adds random noise at every step of the chain [35]. These chains can be interpreted as particular discretizations of SDEs, such as Euler–Maruyama in the case of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm. These SDEs correspond to Fokker–Planck equations [34], which are ODEs in density space, which in turn correspond to score-based particle evolutions based on Liouville equations [26]. Here, the score function is defined by the gradient of the log density.

Deviating from MCMC methods, score-based methods which crucially require knowledge of the score of the distribution at any given time-step. The difficulty manifests as at each time step, only an empirical measure is known, from which the score has to be approximated. Various methods of score approximation include kernel density estimation [6, 49], adaptive kernels [50, 47, 5], and approximation using neural networks [4, 8, 32]. However, many such methods suffer from mode collapse and parameter/initialization sensitivity [41, 30, 14].

Recently, [45] proposed a noise-free sampling based on the regularized Wasserstein proximal operator (RWPO), called the backwards regularized Wasserstein proximal (BRWP) method. In this case, the score is approximated using the score of the RWPO, which is shown to correspond to a semi-implicit discretization of a Fokker–Planck equation. Similarly to the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA), and unlike Langevin algorithms involving Metropolis steps (such as the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm MALA), BRWP can be shown to preserve the Gaussianity of a distribution at each iteration for quadratic target potentials. In particular, in continuous time, the mixing time dependency on dimension dd in the Gaussian case scales only as 𝒪⁡(log⁡(d))\mathcal{O}(\log(d)), whereas ULA scales as 𝒪⁡(d3)\mathcal{O}(d^{3}) and MALA as 𝒪⁡(d2)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}). For low dimensional distributions, the particles evolved through BRWP were found to be structured, with the outermost particles appearing to lie on level-set contours.

The BRWP method has also been extended with tensor-train techniques [19], as well as to the non-smooth Bayesian LASSO problem by using L1L^{1}-splittings based on the Laplace approximation [18]. On the theoretical side, [45] originally demonstrate linear convergence in total variation for quadratic potentials in the continuous case. [17] further extend this to strongly log-concave distributions and smooth initial distributions, showing that the BRWP iterations with equal regularization parameter and time-step indeed form a first-order method for the Fokker–Planck equation.

In this work, we aim to accelerate convergence of BRWP by utilizing preconditioners. The contributions of this work are as follows:

  1. 1.

    In Section 3, we derive the coupled PDE system that we wish to subsequently discretize. Utilizing similar techniques to [29], we demonstrate that the Laplacian regularizations in the Benamou–Brenier formulation of the Wasserstein proximal may be suitably replaced with second-order terms involving the preconditioning matrix. This is derived using a Cole–Hopf transform on a pair of forward-backward anisotropic heat equations.

  2. 2.

    In Section 4 we propose the preconditioned BRWP (PBRWP) method in Algorithm 1. This is given by taking a backwards Euler discretization on the Fokker–Planck component of the PDE derived in the previous section. This yields a semi-implicit discretization of the Liouville equation. We provide expressions for the score approximation in the case of finitely many particles as an interacting particle system. Section 4.1 interprets the interactions as a modified self-attention block, which implicitly allows for efficient parallel computation using common GPU libraries.

  3. 3.

    In the case of Gaussian initial and target measures (corresponding to the infinite-particle limit), Section 5 provides a non-asymptotic analysis of the convergence rate in the discrete step-size regime. This characterizes the convergence rates in terms of the regularization parameter and the preconditioning matrix. We additionally provide various properties such as maximum allowable regularization parameters, Wasserstein contraction, a mean-variance contraction-diffusion inequality, and a maximum norm bound based on the number of particles.

  4. 4.

    In Section 6, the proposed PBRWP method is compared on a variety of toy examples, a Bayesian imaging problem, and Bayesian neural network training. We additionally introduce some heuristic modifications to improve the performance of PBRWP in high dimension scenarios, corresponding to scaling laws in attention-based models. We observe in low dimensions that the proposed method converges faster and stably in KL divergence and maintains the structured particle phenomenon of BRWP. We find rapid convergence to the MAP estimator in while maintaining deviations between particles for Bayesian image deconvolution, and convergence to better trained networks compared to other score-based MCMC methods.

2 Background and Notation

This section covers some basic definitions, including Wasserstein spaces, the Benamou–Brenier PDE formulation, and the non-preconditioned regularized Wasserstein proximal.

Throughout, M∈ℝd×dM\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a symmetric positive definite matrix M∈Sym+⁣+​(ℝd)M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{++}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). We define the scaled norms and inner product on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} as

⟨u,v⟩M=u⊤M−1v,∥⋅∥M2=⟨⋅,⋅⟩M.\langle u,v\rangle_{M}=u^{\top}M^{-1}v,\quad\|\cdot\|_{M}^{2}=\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{M}. (2)
Definition 1 ([39]).

Let 𝒫2​(ℝd){\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be the of probability densities with finite second moment. For μ,ν∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu,\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), the Wasserstein-2 distance 𝒲2​(μ,ν){\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\mu,\nu) is

𝒲2​(μ,ν)=infπ∈Γ⁡(μ,ν)∫‖x−y‖2​dπ⁡(x,y),{\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\mu,\nu)=\inf_{\pi\in\Gamma(\mu,\nu)}\int\|x-y\|^{2}\differential\pi({x},{y}), (3)

where the infimum is taken over couplings π∈Γ⁡(μ,ν)\pi\in\Gamma(\mu,\nu), i.e. probability measures on ℝd×ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfying

∫ℝdπ⁡(x,y)​dy=μ⁡(x),∫ℝdπ⁡(x,y)​dx=ν⁡(y).\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\pi(x,y)\differential{y}=\mu(x),\,\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\pi(x,y)\differential{x}=\nu(y). (4)

Consider a probability density ρ0∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\rho_{0}\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and V∈𝒞1​(ℝd)V\in\mathcal{C}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be a bounded potential function. For a scalar T>0T>0, the Wasserstein proximal of ρ0\rho_{0} is defined as

WProxT,V(ρ0)≔arg​minq∈𝒫2​(ℝd)∫ℝdV(x)q(x)dx+𝒲​(ρ0,q)22​T.\wprox_{T,V}(\rho_{0})\coloneqq\argmin_{q\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V(x)q(x)\differential{x}+\frac{{\mathcal{W}}(\rho_{0},q)^{2}}{2T}. (5)

The Wasserstein proximal can be equivalently reformulated as a coupled PDE system, sometimes known as the Benamou–Brenier or dynamical formulation [2]. Using this, [29] defines the regularized Wasserstein proximal by adding a diffusive term to the continuity equation of the Benamou–Brenier formulation. The resulting mean-field control problem is

infρ,v,q∫0T∫ℝd12​‖v⁡(t,x)‖2​ρ​(t,x)​dx​dt+∫ℝdV⁡(x)​q​(x)​dx,\displaystyle\inf_{\rho,v,q}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1}{2}\|v(t,x)\|^{2}\rho(t,x)\differential{x}\differential{t}+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V(x)q(x)\differential{x}, (6a)
∂tρ⁡(t,x)+∇⋅(ρ⁡(t,x)​v​(t,x))=β−1​Δ​ρ​(t,x),ρ⁡(0,x)=ρ0​(x),ρ⁡(T,x)=q⁡(x).\displaystyle\partial_{t}\rho(t,x)+\nabla\cdot(\rho(t,x)v(t,x))=\beta^{-1}\Delta\rho(t,x),\quad\rho(0,x)=\rho_{0}(x),\,\rho(T,x)=q(x). (6b)

From this problem, the regularized Wasserstein proximal operator (RWPO) WProxT,V\wprox_{T,V} is defined as the solution density function ρ\rho of eq. 6. Taking the regularization parameter β=0\beta=0 recovers the Wasserstein proximal eq. 5 through the Benamou–Brenier formulation of the Wasserstein distance. The RWPO admits the following coupled PDE formulation, consisting of a forward-time Fokker-Planck equation in ρ\rho, and a backward-time viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equation in a dual variable Φ\Phi,

∂tρ⁡(t,x)+∇x⋅(ρ⁡(t,x)​∇xΦ​(t,x))=β−1​Δx​ρ​(t,x),\displaystyle\partial_{t}\rho(t,x)+\nabla_{x}\cdot\left(\rho(t,x)\nabla_{x}\Phi(t,x)\right)=\beta^{-1}\Delta_{x}\rho(t,x), (7a)

ρ⁡(0,x)=ρ0​(x),Φ⁡(T,x)=−V⁡(x).\displaystyle\rho(0,x)=\rho_{0}(x),\quad\Phi(T,x)=-V(x). (7c)

3 Preconditioned Regularized Wasserstein Proximal

We have seen that the regularized Wasserstein proximal is a particular Laplacian regularization of the Benamou–Brenier formulation, corresponding to coupled heat equations and computable using a kernel formula [29]. In this section, we define a geometry-aware elliptic regularization to the Benamou–Brenier formulation, corresponding to coupled anisotropic heat equations under a Cole–Hopf transformation. This manifests as computation with a scaled heat kernel, allowing for more generality in the proximal operator.

From here onwards, let M∈ℝd×dM\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be a symmetric positive definite matrix M∈Sym+⁣+​(ℝd)M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{++}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Define the anisotropic heat kernel

Gt,M​(x,y)≔1(4​π​β−1​t)d/2​|M|1/2​e−β​(x−y)⊤​M−1​(x−y)4​t.G_{t,M}(x,y)\coloneqq\frac{1}{(4\pi\beta^{-1}t)^{d/2}|M|^{1/2}}e^{-\beta\frac{(x-y)^{\top}M^{-1}(x-y)}{4t}}. (11)

This is a scaled version of the standard heat kernel, and it is also a Green’s function for an anisotropic heat equation.

Proposition 2.

The anisotropic kernel Gt,MG_{t,M} is a Green’s function for the following PDE:

{∂tu−β−1∇⋅(M∇u)=0,u⁡(0,x)=δ⁡(y).\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u-\beta^{-1}\nabla\cdot(M\nabla u)=0,\\ u(0,x)=\delta(y).\end{cases}

Proof.

This is from a direct computation. The boundary condition arises from a change of variables with the standard heat kernel. The derivation can be found in A.1.

We now define the preconditioned regularized Wasserstein proximal operator as the terminal time solution to a particular set of PDEs. Then, we show that it is equivalently a convolution involving another inhomogeneous kernel, with the kernel itself defined as a convolution with the anisotropic heat kernel.

Definition 3.

For a symmetric positive definite matrix MM, define the preconditioned regularized Wasserstein proximal operator (PRWPO) WProxT,VM:ρ0↦ρT\wprox^{M}_{T,V}:\rho_{0}\mapsto\rho_{T} to be the terminal density of the following PDE system

{∂tρ(t,x)+∇⋅(ρ(t,x)∇Φ(t,M−1x))=β−1∇⋅(M∇ρ)(t,x),∂tΦ⁡(t,M−1​x)+12​‖∇Φ​(t,M−1​x)‖M2=−β−1​Tr⁡(M−1​(∇2Φ)​(t,M−1​x)),ρ(0,x)=ρ0(x),Φ(T,M−1x)=−V(x).\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\rho(t,x)+\nabla\cdot(\rho(t,x)\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x))=\beta^{-1}\nabla\cdot(M\nabla\rho)(t,x),\\ \partial_{t}\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)+\frac{1}{2}\|\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)\|_{M}^{2}=-\beta^{-1}\Tr(M^{-1}(\nabla^2 \Phi)(t, M^{-1}x)),\\ \rho(0,x)=\rho_{0}(x),\quad\Phi(T,M^{-1}x)=-V(x).\end{cases} (12)

Equivalently, the density of WProxT,VM​ρ0\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\rho_{0} is given by

ρ⁡(T,x)=∫ℝdK⁡(x,y,β,M,T,V)​ρ​(0,y)​dy,\displaystyle\rho(T,x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K(x,y,\beta,M,T,V)\rho(0,y)\differential{y}, (13)

where the normalized kernel is given by

K⁡(x,y,β,M,T,V)≔e−β2​(V​(x)+‖x−y‖M22​T)∫ℝde−β2​(V​(z)+‖z−y‖M22​T)​dz.K(x,y,\beta,M,T,V)\coloneqq\frac{e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(V(x)+\frac{\|x-y\|^{2}_{M}}{2T})}}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(V(z)+\frac{\|z-y\|^{2}_{M}}{2T})}\differential{z}}.

+β24ρ∇Φ(t,M−1x)⊤M−1∇Φ(t,M−1x)e−βΦ(t,M−1x)/2.\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{\beta^{2}}{4}\rho\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)^{\top}M^{-1}\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)e^{-\beta\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)/2}.

Applying the transformation to the forward heat equation in η^\hat{\eta} yields

∂tρ−β2​ρ​∂tΦ⁡(t,M−1​x)\displaystyle\partial_{t}\rho-\frac{\beta}{2}\rho\partial_{t}\Phi(t,M^{-1}x) =β−1∇⋅(M∇ρ)−⟨∇ρ,∇Φ(t,M−1x)⟩\displaystyle=\beta^{-1}\nabla\cdot(M\nabla\rho)-\langle\nabla\rho,\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)\rangle
−12​ρ​Tr⁡(M−1​∇2Φ​(t,M−1​x))+β4​ρ​‖∇Φ​(t,M−1​x)‖M.\displaystyle\qquad-\frac{1}{2}\rho\Tr(M^{-1}\nabla^2 \Phi(t, M^{-1}x))+\frac{\beta}{4}\rho\|\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)\|_{M}.

Simplifying with the Hamilton–Jacobi equation for Φ\Phi eq. 16, we obtain

∂tρ+⟨∇ρ,∇Φ(t,M−1x)⟩+ρTr⁡(M−1​∇2Φ​(t,M−1​x))=β−1∇⋅(M∇ρ)\displaystyle\partial_{t}\rho+\langle\nabla\rho,\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)\rangle+\rho\Tr(M^{-1}\nabla^2 \Phi(t, M^{-1}x))=\beta^{-1}\nabla\cdot(M\nabla\rho)
⇒∂tρ+∇⋅(ρ(t,x)∇Φ(t,M−1x))=β−1∇⋅(M∇ρ).\displaystyle\Rightarrow\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho(t,x)\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x))=\beta^{-1}\nabla\cdot(M\nabla\rho).

This is the desired (modified) Fokker–Planck equation in eq. 12. We have demonstrated that the Cole–Hopf transformation eq. 15 transforms the coupled anisotropic heat equations eq. 14 into a diffusive coupled PDE system: a forward-time Fokker–Planck equation, and a backward-time Hamilton–Jacobi equation. Going backwards, we may infer that the coupled system admits a kernel solution corresponding to the anisotropic heat equation, and showing equivalence in Definition 3. We summarize this in the following proposition.

Proposition 4.

The coupled PDE system

{∂tρ(t,x)+∇⋅(ρ(t,x)∇Φ(t,M−1x))=β−1∇⋅(M∇ρ)(t,x),∂tΦ⁡(t,M−1​x)+12​‖∇Φ​(t,M−1​x)‖M2=−β−1​Tr⁡(M−1​(∇2Φ)​(t,M−1​x)),ρ(0,x)=ρ0(x),Φ(T,M−1x)=−V(x),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\rho(t,x)+\nabla\cdot(\rho(t,x)\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x))=\beta^{-1}\nabla\cdot(M\nabla\rho)(t,x),\\ \partial_{t}\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)+\frac{1}{2}\|\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)\|_{M}^{2}=-\beta^{-1}\Tr(M^{-1}(\nabla^2 \Phi)(t, M^{-1}x)),\\ \rho(0,x)=\rho_{0}(x),\quad\Phi(T,M^{-1}x)=-V(x),\end{cases} (17)

admits the following kernel formulation, where Gt,M​(x,y)G_{t,M}(x,y) is given in eq. 11:

{ρ(t,x)=(GT−t,M∗e−βV/2)(x)⋅(Gt,M∗ρ0(GT,M∗e−βV/2))(x),Φ(t,x)=2β−1log(GT−t,M∗e−βV/2)(Mx).\begin{cases}\rho(t,x)=\left(G_{T-t,M}*e^{-\beta V/2}\right)(x)\cdot\left(G_{t,M}*\frac{\rho_{0}}{(G_{T,M}*e^{-\beta V/2})}\right)(x),\\ \Phi(t,x)=2\beta^{-1}\log\left(G_{T-t,M}*e^{-\beta V/2}\right)(Mx).\end{cases} (18)

Proof.

The PDEs under the change of variables eq. 15 becomes the decoupled anisotropic heat equations eq. 14. Using the Green’s function, the solutions are given by

η(t,x)=GT−t,M∗ηT=(GT−t,M∗e−βV/2)(x).\eta(t,x)=G_{T-t,M}*\eta_{T}=(G_{T-t,M}*e^{-\beta V/2})(x).

From the initial boundary conditions,

η^​(0,x)=ρ0​(x)(GT,M∗e−βV/2)(x).\hat{\eta}(0,x)=\frac{\rho_{0}(x)}{(G_{T,M}*e^{-\beta V/2})(x)}.

From the Green’s function again,

η^​(t,x)=(Gt,M∗ρ0(GT,M∗e−βV/2))​(x).\hat{\eta}(t,x)=\left(G_{t,M}*\frac{\rho_{0}}{(G_{T,M}*e^{-\beta V/2})}\right)(x).

Since ρ=η​η^\rho=\eta\hat{\eta} from eq. 15,

ρ(t,x)=(GT−t,M∗e−βV/2)(x)⋅(Gt,M∗ρ0(GT,M∗e−βV/2))(x).\rho(t,x)=\left(G_{T-t,M}*e^{-\beta V/2}\right)(x)\cdot\left(G_{t,M}*\frac{\rho_{0}}{(G_{T,M}*e^{-\beta V/2})}\right)(x). (19)

In particular, plugging in t=Tt=T, we have the following kernel formula for the PRWPO which is defined as the terminal solution.

Corollary 5.

The preconditioned regularized Wasserstein proximal admits the kernel formula:

WProxT,VM​ρ0​(x)\displaystyle\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\rho_{0}(x) =e−βV(x)/2∫ℝdGT,M​(y,x)​ρ0​(y)(GT,M∗e−βV/2)(y)dy\displaystyle=e^{-\beta V(x)/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{G_{T,M}(y,x)\rho_{0}(y)}{(G_{T,M}*e^{-\beta V/2})(y)}\differential y
=∫ℝdK⁡(x,y,β,M,T,V)​ρ​(0,y)​dy,\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K(x,y,\beta,M,T,V)\rho(0,y)\differential{y}, (20)

where

K⁡(x,y,β,M,T,V)≔e−β2​(V​(x)+‖x−y‖M22​T)∫ℝde−β2​(V​(z)+‖z−y‖M22​T)​dz.K(x,y,\beta,M,T,V)\coloneqq\frac{e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(V(x)+\frac{\|x-y\|^{2}_{M}}{2T})}}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(V(z)+\frac{\|z-y\|^{2}_{M}}{2T})}\differential{z}}. (21)

Note that the PRWPO operator is well defined. The parabolic heat equations given by the Cole–Hopf transform are well defined for all time. Therefore, any probability density will map to a unique output, and moreover the mapping is continuous according to the regularity of the heat equations.

For notation purposes, we shorten the kernel eq. 21 to KM​(x,y)K_{M}(x,y). We may interpret KMK_{M} as a Markov kernel: for any yy, ∫xKM​(x,y)​dx=1\int_{x}K_{M}(x,y)\differential{x}=1, and moreover KMK_{M} is measurable. This is useful to determine how each particle affects the score, given by applying KMK_{M} to a Dirac mass.

4 Preconditioned Backwards Regularized Wasserstein Proximal Method

Equipped with a preconditioned version of the regularized Wasserstein proximal operator, we can proceed like in [45] and devise a sampling algorithm based on the Fokker–Planck component of the coupled PDEs. The Fokker–Planck component can be written as

∂tρ(t,x)+∇⋅(ρ(t,x)∇Φ(t,M−1x)−β−1Mρ∇(logρ)(t,x))=0.\partial_{t}\rho(t,x)+\nabla\cdot\left(\rho(t,x)\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)-\beta^{-1}M\rho\nabla(\log\rho)(t,x)\right)=0. (22)

Using Liouville’s equation with the Hamiltonian ∇Φ(t,M−1x)−β−1M∇(logρ)(x)\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)-\beta^{-1}M\nabla(\log\rho)(x), the corresponding particle formulation with density satisfying eq. 22 is

dXdt=∇Φ(t,M−1X)−β−1M∇logρ(t,X).\frac{\differential X}{\differential t}=\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}X)-\beta^{-1}M\nabla\log\rho(t,X). (23)

This can be seen to approximate the original Liouville equation since ∇Φ​(t,M−1​x)≈−M​V​(x)\nabla\Phi(t,M^{-1}x)\approx-MV(x). Performing a backwards Euler discretization on this ODE, we define the following preconditioned backward regularized Wasserstein proximal (PBRWP) method:

Xk+1=Xk+η(−M∇V(Xk)−β−1M∇logWProxT,VMρk(Xk)),X_{k+1}=X_{k}+\eta\left(-M\nabla V(X_{k})-\beta^{-1}M\nabla\log\wprox_{T,V}^{M}\rho_{k}(X_{k})\right), (24)

where WProxT,VM​ρk\wprox_{T,V}^{M}\rho_{k} is the PRWPO of the distribution of XkX_{k} as given in eq. 17. As in [45], this can be evaluated using the kernel formula eq. 21.

Note that the formal limit as T→0T\rightarrow 0 and η→0\eta\rightarrow 0 is the score-based ODE with potential VV,

dXdt=−M∇V(X)−β−1M∇logρ(X),\frac{\differential X}{\differential{t}}=-M\nabla V(X)-\beta^{-1}M\nabla\log\rho(X), (25)

which has a stationary solution π∝exp⁡(−β​V)\pi\propto\exp(-\beta V).

Based on eq. 24 and the kernel formulation eq. 21, we proceed as in [45] and consider the case where the input ρk\rho_{k} to the regularized Fokker–Planck equation is given by an empirical measure. This arises when updating a collection of points that together approximate the underlying distribution.

Suppose that ρk\rho_{k} is a uniform mixture of Dirac masses at points {𝐱1(k),…,𝐱N(k)}\{{\mathbf{x}}_{1}^{(k)},...,{\mathbf{x}}_{N}^{(k)}\}. From the kernel formulation eq. 21, we have the following expressions to compute the score (dropping the kk superscripts):

WProxT,VM​ρk​(𝐱i)=1N​∑j=1NKM​(𝐱i,𝐱j)=1N​∑j=1Nexp⁡[−β2​(V⁡(𝐱i)+‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖M22​T)]𝒵⁡(𝐱j),\begin{split}\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\rho_{k}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})&=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}K_{M}({\mathbf{x}}_{i},{\mathbf{x}}_{j})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\exp\left[-\frac{\beta}{2}\left(V({\mathbf{x}}_{i})+\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|_{M}^{2}}{2T}\right)\right]}{{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j})},\\ \end{split} (26a)
∇WProxMT,Vρk(𝐱i)=1N​∑j=1N(−β2​(∇V​(𝐱i)+M−1​𝐱i−𝐱jT))​exp⁡[−β2​(V⁡(𝐱i)+‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖M22​T)]𝒵⁡(𝐱j),\begin{split}\nabla\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\rho_{k}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})&=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\left(-\frac{\beta}{2}\left(\nabla V({\mathbf{x}}_{i})+M^{-1}\frac{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}}{T}\right)\right)\exp\left[-\frac{\beta}{2}\left(V({\mathbf{x}}_{i})+\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|_{M}^{2}}{2T}\right)\right]}{{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j})},\\ \end{split} (26b)
𝒵⁡(𝐱j)≔∫ℝde−β2​(V​(z)+‖z−𝐱j‖M22​T)​dz.{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j})\coloneqq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(V(z)+\frac{\|z-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|^{2}_{M}}{2T})}\differential{z}. (26c)

We may observe the score ∇log⁡ρ=∇ρρ\nabla\log\rho=\frac{\nabla\rho}{\rho} as a particular weighted sum. Recall the definition of the softmax function: for a vector v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the softmax is the vector given by

softmax⁡(v)=(exp⁡(vi)∑j=1dexp⁡(vj))i=1,…,d,\mathrm{softmax}(v)=\left(\frac{\exp(v_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{d}\exp(v_j)}\right)_{i=1,...,d},

satisfying ∑jsoftmax​(v)j=1\sum_{j}\mathrm{softmax}(v)_{j}=1. We may rewrite the score in terms of the softmax function, which makes it clear that it acts as an inter-particle diffusive term:

∇log⁡WProxT,VM​ρk​(𝐱i)\displaystyle\nabla\log\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\rho_{k}({\mathbf{x}}_{i}) =∇WProxMT,VρkWProxT,VM​ρk​(𝐱i)\displaystyle=\frac{\nabla\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\rho_{k}}{\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\rho_{k}}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})
=∑j=1N(−β2​(∇V​(𝐱i)+M−1​𝐱i−𝐱jT))​exp⁡[−β2​(V⁡(𝐱i)+‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖M22​T)]𝒵⁡(𝐱j)∑j=1Nexp⁡[−β2​(V⁡(𝐱i)+‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖M22​T)]𝒵⁡(𝐱j)\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\left(-\frac{\beta}{2}\left(\nabla V({\mathbf{x}}_{i})+M^{-1}\frac{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}}{T}\right)\right)\exp\left[-\frac{\beta}{2}\left(V({\mathbf{x}}_{i})+\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|_{M}^{2}}{2T}\right)\right]}{{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j})}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\exp\left[-\frac{\beta}{2}\left(V({\mathbf{x}}_{i})+\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|_{M}^{2}}{2T}\right)\right]}{{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j})}}
=−β∇V(𝐱i)2−β2​T​M−1​𝐱i+β​M−12​T​∑j=1Nsoftmax​(Ui,⋅)j​𝐱j,\displaystyle=-\frac{\beta\nabla V({\mathbf{x}}_{i})}{2}-\frac{\beta}{2T}M^{-1}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}+\frac{\beta M^{-1}}{2T}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathrm{softmax}(U_{i,\cdot})_{j}{\mathbf{x}}_{j},

where we define the interaction kernel Ui,j=Ui,j​(𝐱1,…,𝐱N)U_{i,j}=U_{i,j}({\mathbf{x}}_{1},...,{\mathbf{x}}_{N}) as the matrix

Ui,j=−β2​(V⁡(𝐱i)+‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖M22​T)−log⁡𝒵⁡(𝐱j).U_{i,j}=-\frac{\beta}{2}\left(V({\mathbf{x}}_{i})+\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|^{2}_{M}}{2T}\right)-\log{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j}). (27)

From eq. 24 we can write the particle-wise PBRWP iterations

𝐱i(k+1)\displaystyle{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k+1)} =𝐱i(k)+η(−M∇V(𝐱i(k))−β−1M∇logWProxT,VMρk(𝐱i(k)))\displaystyle={\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)}+\eta\left(-M\nabla V({\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)})-\beta^{-1}M\nabla\log\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\rho_{k}({\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)})\right)
=𝐱i(k)−η2M∇V(𝐱i(k))+η2​T(𝐱i(k)−∑j=1Nsoftmax(Ui,⋅(k))j𝐱j(k))\displaystyle={\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)}-\frac{\eta}{2}M\nabla V({\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)})+\frac{\eta}{2T}\left({\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)}-\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathrm{softmax}(U_{i,\cdot}^{(k)})_{j}{\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{(k)}\right)
=𝐱i(k)−η2M∇V(𝐱i(k))+η2​T(∑j=1Nsoftmax(Ui,⋅(k))j(𝐱i(k)−𝐱j(k))).\displaystyle={\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)}-\frac{\eta}{2}M\nabla V({\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)})+\frac{\eta}{2T}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathrm{softmax}(U_{i,\cdot}^{(k)})_{j}({\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{(k)})\right).

We note that since Ui,jU_{i,j} is only used in the softmax function, it is possible to add a constant for each column without changing the dynamics. In particular, we define a simpler matrix Wi,jW_{i,j} such that

softmax​(Ui,⋅)j=softmax​(Wi,⋅)j,\displaystyle\mathrm{softmax}(U_{i,\cdot})_{j}=\mathrm{softmax}(W_{i,\cdot})_{j},

defined by adding constants depending only on the row ii:

Wi,j\displaystyle W_{i,j} ≔Ui,j+β​V​(𝐱i)2\displaystyle\coloneqq U_{i,j}+\frac{\beta V({\mathbf{x}}_{i})}{2}
=−β​‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖M24​β​T−log⁡𝒵⁡(𝐱j).\displaystyle=-\beta\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|_{M}^{2}}{4\beta T}-\log{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j}). (28)

This has the advantage of avoiding one computation of VV, which is already implicitly used in the normalizing constants 𝒵{\mathcal{Z}}. To further simplify, let 𝑿{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}} be the matrix of particles

𝑿=[𝐱1...𝐱N]∈ℝd×N.{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}=\begin{bmatrix}{\mathbf{x}}_{1}&...&{\mathbf{x}}_{N}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}.

The above iteration can thus be written as

𝑿(k+1)=𝑿(k)−η2M∇V(𝑿(k))+η2​T(𝑿(k)−𝑿(k)softmax(W(k))⊤),{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k+1)}={\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)}-\frac{\eta}{2}M\nabla V({\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)})+\frac{\eta}{2T}\left({\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)}-{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)}\mathrm{softmax}(W^{(k)})^{\top}\right), (29)

where ∇V​(𝑿)=[∇V​(𝐱1)...∇V​(𝐱N)]\nabla V({\bm{\mathsfit{X}}})=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla V({\mathbf{x}}_{1})&...&\nabla V({\mathbf{x}}_{N})\end{bmatrix}, WW is defined in eq. 28, and softmax​(W)i,j=softmax​(Wi,⋅)j\mathrm{softmax}(W)_{i,j}=\mathrm{softmax}(W_{i,\cdot})_{j} is a row-stochastic matrix (and therefore, softmax​(W)⊤\mathrm{softmax}(W)^{\top} is a column-stochastic matrix). This formulation has the advantage of being easily parallelizable (or serially computed, depending on memory restrictions), assuming that the normalizing constant can be easily computed. Summarizing, the PBRWP update is given in Algorithm 1, which details the steps used in practice.

Remark 6.

The corresponding limit of eq. 24 as η→0\eta\rightarrow 0 satisfies the modified Fokker–Planck equation

∂tρ=β−1∇⋅(ρM∇logWProxT,VM⁡(ρ)exp⁡(−β​V)).\partial_{t}\rho=\beta^{-1}\nabla\cdot\left(\rho M\nabla\log\frac{\wprox^{M}_{T,V}(\rho)}{\exp(-\beta V)}\right). (30)

A stationary solution is π^\hat{\pi} satisfies WProxT,VM⁡(π^)∝exp⁡(−β​V)\wprox^{M}_{T,V}(\hat{\pi})\propto\exp(-\beta V). This is a semi-implicit discretization of eq. 22, where ρ∇logρ(t,x)\rho\nabla\log\rho(t,x) is replaced with ρ∇logWProxT,VM(ρ)\rho\nabla\log\wprox^{M}_{T,V}(\rho), and the dual variable Φ\Phi is also replaced with the terminal condition Φ⁡(T,M−1​x)=−V⁡(x)\Phi(T,M^{-1}x)=-V(x).

4.1 Transformer reformulation

We may connect eq. 29 to self-attention mechanisms, which are commonly employed in transformers [48], and have recently attracted interpretations as particle evolutions [38, 18]. Recall that an attention block takes the following form: for queries Q∈ℝd×NQ\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}, keys K∈ℝd×NK\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N} and values V∈ℝdV×NV\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{V}\times N} of the prescribed dimensions11 1 The matrices are transposed compared to the literature in order to be consistent with the convention in this work. The usual form is Attn⁡(Q,K,V)=softmax⁡(Q​K⊤d)​V\mathrm{Attn}(Q;K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V, where the softmax is taken row-wise as in this work. Both forms are equivalent.,

Attn⁡(Q,K,V)=V​softmax​(Q⊤​Kd)⊤∈ℝdV×N.\mathrm{Attn}(Q;K,V)=V\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{Q^{\top}K}{\sqrt{d}}\right)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{V}\times N}. (31)

We may connect this with the softmax term in eq. 29. The argument of the softmax eq. 28 is

Wi,j\displaystyle W_{i,j} =−β​‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖M24​T−log⁡𝒵⁡(𝐱j)\displaystyle=-\beta\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|_{M}^{2}}{4T}-\log{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j})
=β​𝐱i⊤​M−1​𝐱j2​T−log⁡𝒵⁡(𝐱j)−β​‖𝐱i‖M2+‖𝐱j‖M24​T.\displaystyle=\beta\frac{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}M^{-1}{\mathbf{x}}_{j}}{2T}-\log{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j})-\beta\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\|^{2}_{M}+\|{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|^{2}_{M}}{4T}.

Discarding the d\sqrt{d} scaling22 2 This will be reintroduced in Section 6.4 as a heuristic modification in high dimensions. of eq. 31 and the constant-in-jj term ‖𝐱i‖M2\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\|_{M}^{2}, the diffusion term 𝑿(K)​softmax​(W(k))⊤{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(K)}\mathrm{softmax}(W^{(k)})^{\top} for NN particles takes the form of masked attention

V​softmax​(Q⊤​K−𝟏​𝐳⊤)⊤,V\mathrm{softmax}\left(Q^{\top}K-\mathbf{1}{\mathbf{z}}^{\top}\right)^{\top}, (32)

where Q⊤​K=β2​T​𝑿⊤​M−1​𝑿Q^{\top}K=\frac{\beta}{2T}{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{\top}M^{-1}{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}, 𝐳∈ℝN{\mathbf{z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} is the vector of normalizing constants 𝐳j=log⁡𝒵⁡(𝐱j)+β​‖𝐱j‖M24​T{\mathbf{z}}_{j}=\log{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j})+\beta\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|_{M}^{2}}{4T}, and V=𝑿V={\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}.

For an input H∈ℝd×NH\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}, the self-attention framework imposes the particular forms V=WV​H,K=WK​H,V=WV​HV=W_{V}H,\,K=W_{K}H,\,V=W_{V}H, where WV,WK∈ℝd×d,WV∈ℝdV×dW_{V},W_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d},\,W_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{V}\times d} are some admissible matrices. By taking H=𝑿H={\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}, the preconditioning arises as WV⊤​WK=M−1W_{V}^{\top}W_{K}=M^{-1}, and WV=IW_{V}=I, making the diffusion in PBRWP interpretable as a modified self-attention.

Remark 7.

In the other direction, modeling transformers as interacting particle systems, [38] consider self-attention transformers with symmetric interaction and an additional condition WQ⊤​WK=WK⊤​WQ=−WVW_{Q}^{\top}W_{K}=W_{K}^{\top}W_{Q}=-W_{V}, demonstrating that transformers can be interpreted as a particular Wasserstein gradient flow, converging to a nonlinear PDE. [13] consider transformers acting on the sphere 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1} in the special case WQ=WK=IW_{Q}=W_{K}=I, presenting various conditions on the dimension, number of particles, and temperature such that particles will cluster. [7] demonstrate well-posedness of the induced PDE for various forms of self-attention, as well as a continuous-time analysis of the Gaussian-preserving properties. These works consider the continuous limit of the transformers to obtain these links.

5 Analysis in Gaussian distributions

In the particular case where V⁡(x)=x⊤​Σ−1​x2V(x)=\frac{x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x}{2}, i.e. the target distribution is 𝒩⁡(0,β−1​Σ){\mathcal{N}}(0,\beta^{-1}\Sigma), the PRWPO and PBRWP iterations can be computed in closed form. Suppose MM is now such that c​M⪯Σ⪯C​McM\preceq\Sigma\preceq CM, where 0<c≤C<∞0<c\leq C<\infty, and T<cT<c. For Gaussian distributions, the PRWPO admits a closed form as follows.

Proposition 8.

For a Gaussian density ρk=𝒩⁡(μk,Σk)\rho_{k}={\mathcal{N}}(\mu_{k},\Sigma_{k}) and the quadratic potential V⁡(x)=x⊤​Σ−1​x/2V(x)=x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x/2, the PRWPO operator satisfies

WProxT,VM⁡(ρk)=𝒩⁡(μ~k,Σ~k),\wprox_{T,V}^{M}(\rho_{k})={\mathcal{N}}(\tilde{\mu}_{k},\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}), (33)

where μ~k,Σ~k\tilde{\mu}_{k},\tilde{\Sigma}_{k} are given by

μ~k=(I+T​M​Σ−1)−1​μk,\displaystyle\tilde{\mu}_{k}=(I+TM\Sigma^{-1})^{-1}\mu_{k}, (34)
Σ~k=2​β−1​T​(T​Σ−1+M−1)−1+(T​Σ−1+M−1)−1​M−1​Σk​M−1​(T​Σ−1+M−1)−1.\displaystyle\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}=2\beta^{-1}T\left(T\Sigma^{-1}+M^{-1}\right)^{-1}+\left(T\Sigma^{-1}+M^{-1}\right)^{-1}M^{-1}\Sigma_{k}M^{-1}\left(T\Sigma^{-1}+M^{-1}\right)^{-1}. (35)

Moreover, the kernel KM​(x,y)K_{M}(x,y) in eq. 21 takes the form of a Gaussian density

KM​(⋅,y)∼𝒩⁡((Σ−12+M−12​T)−1​M−12​T​y,(β​Σ−12​β+β​M−12​T)−1).K_{M}(\cdot,y)\sim{\mathcal{N}}\left(\left(\frac{\Sigma^{-1}}{2}+\frac{M^{-1}}{2T}\right)^{-1}\frac{M^{-1}}{2T}y,\left(\frac{\beta\Sigma^{-1}}{2\beta}+\frac{\beta M^{-1}}{2T}\right)^{-1}\right). (36)

Proof Sketch.

The kernel formula can be computed in closed form for Gaussians, and the product of two Gaussian densities is again proportional to a Gaussian density. The full proof is given in B.2.

Since the PRWPO maps Gaussian distributions to Gaussian distributions, the score function is linear, and the PBRWP iterations also preserve Gaussianity.

Corollary 9.

For a Gaussian density ρk=𝒩⁡(0,Σk)\rho_{k}={\mathcal{N}}(0,\Sigma_{k}), the PBRWP iteration satisfies the update ρk+1=𝒩⁡(0,Σk+1)\rho_{k+1}={\mathcal{N}}(0,\Sigma_{k+1}), where

Σk+1=(I−η​M​Σ−1+η​β−1​M​Σ~k−1)​Σk​(I−η​M​Σ−1+η​β−1​M​Σ~k−1)⊤.\Sigma_{k+1}=(I-\eta M\Sigma^{-1}+\eta\beta^{-1}M\tilde{\Sigma}^{-1}_{k})\Sigma_{k}(I-\eta M\Sigma^{-1}+\eta\beta^{-1}M\tilde{\Sigma}^{-1}_{k})^{\top}. (37)

Proof.

Follows from using Proposition 8 in the PBRWP update eq. 24.

Now that we have shown that the PBRWP iteration preserves Gaussianity, we wish to consider the convergence for discrete time-steps. In the case where the initial and target distributions are both Gaussian, we can show that the distributions generated by PBRWP with discrete step-sizes converge to a Gaussian. Moreover, the terminal distributions are independent of step-size, only depending on TT, the terminal Gaussian and the preconditioner. The following result extends the result of [45] from continuous time to discrete time, as well as adding generality by working in the preconditioned setting. We consider the zero-mean initialization case for brevity, as the covariances do not depend on the mean; moreover, it can be shown that the means of the iterates converge linearly to the target mean.

Theorem 10.

Suppose V⁡(x)=x⊤​Σ−1​x/2V(x)=x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x/2, and fix a β>0\beta>0. For the target distribution π=𝒩⁡(0,β−1​Σ)\pi={\mathcal{N}}(0,\beta^{-1}\Sigma) and positive definite preconditioner MM, let c,C>0c,C>0 be such that c​M⪯Σ⪯C​McM\preceq\Sigma\preceq CM. Let T∈(0,c)T\in(0,c) so that the inverse PRWPO is well-defined. Then there exists a stationary distribution to the discrete-time PBRWP iterations, and it is Gaussian π^=𝒩⁡(0,Σ^)\hat{\pi}={\mathcal{N}}(0,\hat{\Sigma}), satisfying WProxT,VM​π^=π\wprox_{T,V}^{M}\hat{\pi}=\pi. Moreover, it is unique within distributions with sufficiently decaying Fourier transforms.

Suppose further that the initial Gaussian distribution ρ0=𝒩⁡(0,Σ0)\rho_{0}={\mathcal{N}}(0,\Sigma_{0}) has its covariance commuting with Σ\Sigma. Let ρk\rho_{k} be the iterations generated by PBRWP, and let ρ~k=WProxT,VM⁡(ρk)\tilde{\rho}_{k}=\wprox_{T,V}^{M}(\rho_{k}). Further let λ\lambda be such that M−1​Σk​M−1\sqrt{M}^{-1}\Sigma_{k}\sqrt{M}^{-1} are uniformly bounded below by some λ\lambda (which holds as Σk→Σ\Sigma_{k}\rightarrow\Sigma). Let the step-size η\eta be bounded by

η​β−1≤min⁡((maxi⁡|λi​(Ξ~k−1−Ξ~∞−1)|)−1/2,3​λmin​(Ξ~k)/32)\eta\beta^{-1}\leq\min((\max_{i}|\lambda_{i}(\tilde{\Xi}_{k}^{-1}-\tilde{\Xi}_{\infty}^{-1})|)^{-1}/2,3\lambda_{\min}(\tilde{\Xi}_{k})/32)

Then the exact discrete-time PBRWP method has the following decay in KL divergence:

DKL(ρ~k+1∥π)−DKL(ρ~k∥π)≤−η2​C​[β+2​T​(1+T​C−1)−1​(1+T​c−1)2​λ−1]DKL(ρ~k∥π).\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\tilde{\rho}_{k+1}\|\pi)-\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\tilde{\rho}_{k}\|\pi)\\ \leq-\frac{\eta}{2C[\beta+2\ T(1+TC^{-1})^{-1}(1+Tc^{-1})^{2}\lambda^{-1}]}\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\tilde{\rho}_{k}\|\pi). (38)

Sketch Proof.

From the condition, there exists a (Gaussian) distribution 𝒩⁡(0,Σ^){\mathcal{N}}(0,\hat{\Sigma}) such that WProxT,VM⁡(𝒩⁡(0,Σ^))=𝒩⁡(0,β−1​Σ)\wprox_{T,V}^{M}({\mathcal{N}}(0,\hat{\Sigma}))={\mathcal{N}}(0,\beta^{-1}\Sigma). Uniqueness comes from the closed-form kernel eq. 36 and the invertibility of Gaussian convolution on the range of WProxT,VM\wprox^{M}_{T,V}. Moreover, the PBRWP iterations generate Gaussian distributions, with closed-form covariance updates. The KL divergence between two Gaussians has a closed form in terms of the means and covariances, from which the decay comes using a Taylor expansion. The full proof is given in B.3.

5.1 Additional properties

We briefly list some properties of the PRWPO and PBRWP, and refer to appendix C for more detailed statements and proofs.

  1. 1.

    Conditions for PRWPO invertibility. For a density ρ\rho, there exists a unique distribution ρ0\rho_{0} such that ρ=WProxT,VM​ρ0\rho=\wprox_{T,V}^{M}\rho_{0} if and only if ρ⁡(x)​eβ​V​(x)/2\rho(x)e^{\beta V(x)/2} has Fourier transform decaying at least as fast than e−T​β−1​ξ⊤​M​ξe^{-T\beta^{-1}\xi^{\top}M\xi}. In the Gaussian case V=x⊤​Σ−1​x/2V=x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x/2, this is equivalent to Σ⪰T​M\Sigma\succeq TM.

  2. 2.

    The regularized Wasserstein proximal is a 𝒲2{\mathcal{W}}_{2} contraction. For quadratic VV, let ζ≔(C−12+12​T)−1​(12​T)<1\zeta\coloneqq(\frac{C^{-1}}{2}+\frac{1}{2T})^{-1}(\frac{1}{2T})<1, where CC is as in Theorem 10. For any μ,ν\mu,\nu in Wasserstein-2 space,

    𝒲2​(WProxT,VM​μ,WProxT,VM​ν)≤ζ​𝒲2​(μ,ν).{\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\mu,\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\nu)\leq\zeta{\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\mu,\nu). (39)
  3. 3.

    Mean-variance tradeoff. For strongly convex VV and any β>0\beta>0, the particles move together towards the minimizer, at a rate balanced between the inter-particle variance and the distances to the minimizer. In particular, let x^\hat{x} be the minimizer of VV, and let 𝑿^=[x^...x^]=x^​𝟏N⊤∈ℝd×N\hat{{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}}=\begin{bmatrix}\hat{x}&...&\hat{x}\end{bmatrix}=\hat{x}\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}. In particular, suppose VV is μ\mu-relatively strongly convex with respect to MM. Then for any 𝑿∈ℝd×N{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N},

    ⟨Δ,M−1​(𝑿−𝑿^)⟩Frob≤‖𝑿−𝑿^‖2,M​(−μ2​‖𝑿−𝑿^‖2,M+(1+N)2​T​‖𝑿−1N​𝑿​𝟏N​𝟏N⊤‖2,M).\langle\Delta,M^{-1}({\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}-\hat{{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}})\rangle_{\text{Frob}}\\ \leq\|{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}-\hat{{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}}\|_{2,M}\left(-\frac{\mu}{2}\|{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}-\hat{{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}}\|_{2,M}+\frac{(1+\sqrt{N})}{2T}\|{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}-\frac{1}{N}{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}\mathbf{1}_{N}\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\top}\|_{2,M}\right).
  4. 4.

    Diffusion is bounded based on number of particles. For quadratic V=x⊤​Σ−1​x/2V=x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x/2, suppose M=ΣM=\Sigma (and T<1T<1). Suppose that 𝐱1{\mathbf{x}}_{1} is an exterior point of the convex hull of {𝐱i}\{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\}, and further that δ>0\delta>0 is such that for all j≠1j\neq 1,

    𝐱1⊤​M−1​𝐱j≤𝐱1⊤​M−1​𝐱1−δ​‖𝐱1‖M.{\mathbf{x}}_{1}^{\top}M^{-1}{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\leq{\mathbf{x}}_{1}^{\top}M^{-1}{\mathbf{x}}_{1}-\delta\|{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\|_{M}. (40)

    Then, if 𝐱1{\mathbf{x}}_{1} has sufficiently large norm, in particular assuming,

    δ​‖𝐱1‖M≥2​β−1​T​log⁡(2​(N−1)T),\delta\|{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\|_{M}\geq 2\beta^{-1}T\log(\frac{2 (N-1)}{T}), (41)

    then for small step-size, the updated point satisfies ‖𝐱1(k+1)‖M<‖𝐱1(k)‖M\|{\mathbf{x}}_{1}^{(k+1)}\|_{M}<\|{\mathbf{x}}_{1}^{(k)}\|_{M}. In other words, the norm of the outermost particle scales at most as 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log N).

6 Experiments

In this section, we present various two-dimensional toy examples to demonstrate the effects of adding a preconditioning matrix on the sampling behavior, followed by high-dimensional Bayesian total-variation regularized image deconvolution, and Bayesian neural network training. We compare against the MCMC-based baselines ULA, MALA and the mirror Langevin algorithm (MLA) [21, 23] for the low-dimensional examples, and various kernel-based methods to be detailed for the Bayesian neural network experiment. Throughout, we fix β=1\beta=1.

6.1 Gaussian low particle regime

We first consider the evolution of (P)BRWP for the two-dimensional standard Gaussian 𝒩⁡(0,I2){\mathcal{N}}(0,I_{2}), with the identity preconditioner M=IM=I. In this case, for a fixed T∈(0,1)T\in(0,1), Theorem 10 gives that the RWPO (with parameter TT) of the iterated distributions should approach 𝒩⁡(0,I2){\mathcal{N}}(0,I_{2}). Moreover, the RWPO for this quadratic distribution is given by the closed-form Gaussian kernel eq. 36. In particular, each point gets mapped into a Gaussian with covariance (12+12​T)−1​I(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2T})^{-1}I.

Figure 1 demonstrates the density evolution of the RWPO of the (P)BRWP iterations, evaluated with 5 particles, regularization T=0.2T=0.2 and step-size η=0.1\eta=0.1. We observe as expected from Theorem 10 that the RWPO converges to that of the standard Gaussian, even in the finite particle setting. Figure 2 demonstrates the effect of the number of particles from 3 to 6, evaluated at convergence at iteration 100 and with the same parameters above. In particular, we observe that the contours of the RWPO are initially triangular, then square and pentagonal, gradually becoming smoother and better approximating the standard Gaussian. We observe as well in the 6-particle case that while the contour is pentagonal, the density is more rounded at the origin, indicating that there is one particle there surrounded by 5 other particles.

6.2 Bimodal distribution

As a non-convex potential, we consider the two-moons bimodal distribution as given in [50, 45],

p⁡(x)∝exp⁡(−2​(‖x‖−3)2)⁡[exp⁡(−2​(x1−3)2)+exp⁡(−2​(x1+3)2)].p(x)\propto\exp(-2(\|x\|-3)^2)\left[\exp(-2(x_1-3)^2)+\exp(-2(x_1+3)^2)\right].

This is generated by the potential VV with corresponding gradient ∇V\nabla V as follows:

V⁡(x)\displaystyle V(x) =2​(‖x‖−3)2−2​log⁡[exp⁡(−2​(x1−3)2)+exp⁡(−2​(x1+3)2)],\displaystyle=2(\|x\|-3)^{2}-2\log\left[\exp(-2(x_1-3)^2)+\exp(-2(x_1+3)^2)\right], (42a)
∇V​(x)\displaystyle\nabla V(x) =4​(‖x‖−3)​x‖x‖+4​(x1−3)​exp⁡(−2​(x1−3)2)+4​(x1+3)​exp⁡(−2​(x1+3)2)exp⁡(−2​(x1−3)2)+exp⁡(−2​(x1+3)2)​e1,\displaystyle=4\frac{(\|x\|-3)x}{\|x\|}+\frac{4(x_{1}-3)\exp(-2(x_1-3)^2)+4(x_{1}+3)\exp(-2(x_1+3)^2)}{\exp(-2(x_1-3)^2)+\exp(-2(x_1+3)^2)}\mathrm{e}_{1}, (42b)

where e1\mathrm{e}_{1} is the first standard basis vector. We consider a low-variance initialization and a high-variance initialization. For the low-variance initialization, we consider the same setup as [45], where the particles are initially distributed as 𝒩⁡(0,I){\mathcal{N}}(0,I); for the high-variance setup, the initial distribution is 𝒩⁡(0,6​I){\mathcal{N}}(0,6I). Figure 3 demonstrates that in this case, adding preconditioning has minimal effect on the convergence rate of BRWP and PBRWP, and indeed leads to a slightly higher bias. The bias can be seen qualitatively in Figure 4, which demonstrates that the particles retain the same structured behavior at convergence, but takes a different path at small iterations.

We observe a different compression phenomenon with the high-variance initialization, when the samples are initially distributed around the modes instead of between the modes. Figure 5 demonstrates that in this case, the preconditioning has a significant acceleration effect, where the KL divergence decreases faster than BRWP. Moreover, Figure 6 demonstrates that PBRWP particles are less noisy than BRWP particles at low iterations.

6.3 Annulus

Consider the two-dimensional annulus defined with the potential

V⁡(x)=(‖(1002)​x‖−3)2,∇V​(x)=2​‖(1002)​x‖−3‖(1002)​x‖​(1002)2​x.\displaystyle V(x)=\left(\left\|\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&2\end{pmatrix}x\right\|-3\right)^{2},\quad\nabla V(x)=2\frac{\left\|\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&2\end{pmatrix}x\right\|-3}{\left\|\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&2\end{pmatrix}x\right\|}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&2\end{pmatrix}^{2}x. (43)

We consider M=diag⁡([4,1])M=\diag([4,1]), which takes into account the scaling of the annulus in both directions. The initialization is taken to be the off-center Gaussian 𝒩⁡((2,2),I){\mathcal{N}}((2,2),I), and the particles should diffuse along the elliptical potential well. Figure 7 shows the evolution of various methods from this initialization, evaluated with 100 particles. We observe that the preconditioned methods MLA and PBRWP are able to diffuse faster than their non-preconditioned counterparts, namely covering the annulus at iteration 50. Figure 8 verifies this quantitatively, where the PBRWP particles converge significantly faster than BRWP, and to a lower minimum than the Langevin methods.

6.4 High dimensional examples and modifications

In high dimensions, approximating the normalizing constant with a Monte Carlo integral is highly inaccurate [45]. This manifests empirically as non-interaction between particles, or excessive interaction leading to diverging particles. Therefore, we require another approximation using Laplace’s method [3], similarly to [18, 17]. This approximation has also been used in the other direction, e.g. [46] using integrals to approximate infimal convolutions.

Laplace’s method consists of the following approximation: for a 𝒞2{\mathcal{C}}^{2} function ff and a continuous function gg, assume that ff has a unique global minimizer x∗x^{*} and satisfies some coercivity condition. Then, we have the following approximation:

det⁡(∇2f​(x∗))​exp⁡(f⁡(x∗)/T)(2​π​T)d/2​∫ℝdg⁡(x)​exp(−f(x)/T)​dx→g⁡(x∗)as ​T→0+.\sqrt{\det(\nabla^2 f(x^*))}\frac{\exp(f(x^*)/T)}{(2\pi T)^{d/2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}g(x)\exp(-f(x)/T)\differential{x}\rightarrow g(x^{*})\quad\text{as }T\rightarrow 0^{+}. (44)

Applying this with f⁡(x)=β​‖x−𝐱j‖M2/4f(x)=\beta\|x-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|_{M}^{2}/4 and g⁡(x)=exp(−βV(x)/2)g(x)=\exp(-\beta V(x)/2), we obtain the approximation

𝒵⁡(𝐱j)\displaystyle{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j}) =∫ℝdexp⁡(−β2​(V​(z)−‖z−𝐱j‖M22​T))​dz\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\exp(-\frac{\beta}{2}\left(V(z) - \frac{\|z - \rvx_j\|_{M}^2}{2T}\right))\differential{z} (45)
≈det⁡M​exp⁡(−β2​V​(𝐱j))​C​(β,T),\displaystyle\approx\sqrt{\det M}\exp(-\frac{\beta}{2}V(\rvx_j))C(\beta,T), (46)

where C=C⁡(β,T)C=C(\beta,T) is a constant independent of 𝐱j{\mathbf{x}}_{j}. We note that actually only a Hölder type condition is required for a similar asymptotic to hold, albeit with a different normalizing factor [46, Thm. 2]. Using this, the log⁡𝒵⁡(𝐱j)\log{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j}) term may be approximated by −βV(𝐱j)/2+logC(β,T)+12logdetM-\beta V({\mathbf{x}}_{j})/2+\log C(\beta,T)+\frac{1}{2}\log\det M. For constant MM, the latter two terms will disappear in the softmax. We refer to this as the Laplace approximation in the following section.

In high dimensions, the matching term ‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖M\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\|_{M} can be large for i≠ji\neq j, leading to the interaction matrix softmax​(Ui,⋅)j\mathrm{softmax}(U_{i,\cdot})_{j} being close to identity. Similarly to the seminal work on transformers [48], we additionally propose to set the diffusion parameter as β=d−1/2\beta=d^{-1/2}, which increases the diffusion. We refer to this as scaling in the following section.

The resulting modified iteration using scaling and the Laplace approximation is as follows, where β=d−1/2\beta=d^{-1/2},

𝑿(k+1)=𝑿(k)−η2M∇V(𝑿(k))+η2​T(𝑿(k)−𝑿(k)softmax(W(k))⊤),\displaystyle{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k+1)}={\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)}-\frac{\eta}{2}M\nabla V({\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)})+\frac{\eta}{2T}\left({\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)}-{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)}\mathrm{softmax}(W^{(k)})^{\top}\right), (47a)
Wi,j(k)=−β​‖𝐱i(k)−𝐱j(k)‖M24​T+β2​V​(𝐱j(k)).\displaystyle W_{i,j}^{(k)}=-\beta\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{(k)}\|_{M}^{2}}{4T}+\frac{\beta}{2}V({\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{(k)}). (47b)

6.5 High-dimensional Gaussian distributions

We demonstrate the effect of taking β=d−1/2\beta=d^{-1/2} instead of β=1\beta=1, as well as the Laplace approximation in Figure 9. We test on a 50-dimensional Gaussian with diagonal covariance Σ=diag⁡(0.1,0.2,…,5)\Sigma=\diag(0.1,0.2,...,5) and condition number 50. We let M=ΣM=\Sigma be the preconditioner as before, and plot the particles projected onto the first and last dimensions in the horizontal and vertical directions respectively. Recall that in the Gaussian case, the normalizing constant can be computed exactly in the finite particle setting. We compare PBRWP with step-size η=0.1\eta=0.1, T=0.02,0.2,0.9T=0.02,0.2,0.9, with and without both the scaling and Laplace approximation after convergence at 1000 iteration.

We observe that the Laplace approximation does not seem to qualitatively affect the diffusion behavior of the particles, with or without the β=d−1/2\beta=d^{-1/2} scaling modification. However, the scaling is able to counter the mode-collapse phenomenon that comes with high dimensions. By reducing the scale of the interaction matrix, the particles are able to repel each other from further away. Motivated by this, we use the scaling for high dimensions to avoid mode collapse.

6.6 Deconvolution

We consider the Bayesian problem corresponding to the (convex) total-variation regularized (TV) objective [37],

V⁡(x)=12​σ2​‖A​x−y‖22+λ​TV​(x),V(x)=\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\|Ax-y\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\mathrm{TV}(x), (48)

where AA is a convolution operator, yy is a corrupted image, and TV⁡(x)=‖D​x‖1\mathrm{TV}(x)=\|Dx\|_{1} denotes the discrete total variation functional. For image deconvolution, the forward operator AA takes the form A=ℱ∗​Λ​ℱA={\mathcal{F}}^{*}\Lambda{\mathcal{F}}, where ℱ{\mathcal{F}} is the (complex, unitary) matrix of the discrete Fourier transform, ℱ∗{\mathcal{F}}^{*} is its inverse, and Λ\Lambda is a diagonal matrix. In this case, the Hessian of the first term takes the simple form σ−2​A∗​A=σ−2​ℱ∗​Λ∗​Λ​ℱ\sigma^{-2}A^{*}A=\sigma^{-2}{\mathcal{F}}^{*}\Lambda^{*}\Lambda{\mathcal{F}}. Similarly to SALSA [1], we may use a regularized version as a preconditioner M=(A∗​A+τ​I)−1M=(A^{*}A+\tau I)^{-1}, where τ>0\tau>0 is some constant, taken to be τ=0.5\tau=0.5. We note that sampling from the distribution 𝒩⁡(0,M){\mathcal{N}}(0,M) is possible using the equation M=ℱ∗(Λ∗Λ+τI)−1/2ℱ\sqrt{M}={\mathcal{F}}^{*}(\Lambda^{*}\Lambda+\tau I)^{-1/2}{\mathcal{F}}, which allows for the use of MLA. We further note that using the regularized Hessian (σ2​A∗​A+τ​I)−1(\sigma^{2}A^{*}A+\tau I)^{-1} does not provide adequate preconditioning for PBRWP or MLA, likely due to the ill-conditioning of the TV term with respect to this metric.

We compare the mean and (norm of the channel-wise) standard deviation of the TV-regularized objective. In addition, we compute the PSNR of the finite-particle posterior mean to the true TV-regularized solution, equivalent to running a fixed number of parallel chains for the Langevin methods. We do this to compare the small-particle behavior of the noise-free methods versus the Langevin methods. The minimizer of the objective eq. 48 is computed using subgradient descent for 30,000 iterations, applied with decreasing step-sizes 1​e−{4,5,6}1\mathrm{e}-\{4,5,6\} for 10,000 iterations each. The image considered is the butterfly image from the set3c dataset, which has a dimension of 3×256×2563\times 256\times 256.

We compare against ULA, MLA, and MYULA [11]. We note that the acceptance probability for MALA is almost degenerate for this high-dimensional problem and requires extremely small step-sizes, and is thus omitted due to slow convergence. MYULA takes the following form: for a composite potential of the form exp⁡(−f⁡(x)+g⁡(x))\exp(-f(x) + g(x)), a step-size τ>0\tau>0 and a regularization parameter θ>0\theta>0,

Xk+1=(1−τθ)Xk−τ∇f(Xk)+τθproxθ​g(Xk)+2​τZk+1,X_{k+1}=\left(1-\frac{\tau}{\theta}\right)X_{k}-\tau\nabla f(X_{k})+\frac{\tau}{\theta}\prox_{\theta g}(X_{k})+\sqrt{2\tau}Z_{k+1}, (MYULA)

where Zk+1Z_{k+1} are independent standard Gaussians. This is the unadjusted Langevin algorithm, applied to the regularized potential where gg is replaced by its Moreau–Yosida regularization with parameter θ\theta. Applied to the deconvolution potential eq. 48, we identify f⁡(x)=12​σ2​‖A​x−y‖2f(x)=\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\|Ax-y\|^{2} and g⁡(x)=λ​TV⁡(x)g(x)=\lambda\TV(x). The proximal of gg is computed using the Chambolle–Pock algorithm [9] using the implementation in the DeepInverse Python library [43], and the parameter is fixed as θ=1​e−4\theta=1\mathrm{e}-4.

The step-sizes for the baseline methods are chosen with a grid-search such that the PSNR is maximized after 2000 iterations, and can be found in the appendix. We compare with 40 particles due to GPU memory limitations from the 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) scaling of fully parallelized PBRWP33 3 It is possible to remove some parallelization by computing the interaction matrix column-wise, yielding 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) memory constraint..

The experimental setting differs from typical settings as follows, to highlight the difference between Langevin methods and the noise-free methods BRWP and PBRWP:

  1. 1.

    Low sample count. Langevin algorithms usually run many iterations (around 1​e​51\mathrm{e}5) of the Markov chain to construct an estimate of the posterior mean. In our case, since the samples are approximately convergent for high iterations, taking means over iterations is not insightful, and we replace it with the mean over particles. The particles for Langevin methods can be computed using parallel chains.

  2. 2.

    Short “burn-in” phase. While typical Bayesian imaging methods run burn-in periods for up to 1​e​61\mathrm{e}6 iterations, the noise-free methods again do not benefit from these long iterations. As our objective is rapid convergence, we consider only methods that are able to converge in the short iteration regime.

  3. 3.

    Comparison with MAP estimate. In high dimensions, computing the posterior mean is intractable, and is usually estimated. While it is possible to consider the convergence of the algorithm to the posterior mean by applying a Metropolis–Hastings correction step [16], this would compare the algorithms against an estimator with a-priori unknown uncertainty. We choose the MAP estimate instead as it is computable up to arbitrary accuracy for this convex task, and to compare the mode concentration of the algorithms.

Table 1 plots the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of the particle means, compared to the MAP estimate eq. 48 (equivalently, the minimizer of the potential). We observe that both BRWP and PBRWP converge to much higher values of PSNR, indicating better concentration around the MAP. Moreover, PBRWP has higher PSNR at lower iterations, indicating faster convergence. The lower PSNR of the preconditioned methods compared to the non-preconditioned methods can be explained by the differing noise and diffusion scales. Figure 10 plots the pixel-wise standard deviation of the particles at various iteration counts. We observe again that PBRWP has higher contrast compared to BRWP at low iterations, indicating faster convergence. Moreover, the noise-free methods have very low noise outside the edges. This low-rank phenomenon arises since diffusion comes from inter-particle interactions.

6.7 Bayesian neural networks

In this section, we empirically investigate the possibility of a variable preconditioning matrix MM, applied to a high-dimensional non-convex potential. Recall the PBRWP iteration eq. 29 for particles {𝐱i}i=1N\{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}:

𝑿(k+1)=𝑿(k)−η2M∇V(𝑿(k))+η2​T(𝑿(k)−𝑿(k)softmax(W(k))⊤),\displaystyle{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k+1)}={\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)}-\frac{\eta}{2}M\nabla V({\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)})+\frac{\eta}{2T}\left({\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)}-{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)}\mathrm{softmax}(W^{(k)})^{\top}\right),
Wi,j(k)=−β​‖𝐱i(k)−𝐱j(k)‖M24​T−log⁡𝒵⁡(𝐱j(k)).\displaystyle W_{i,j}^{(k)}=-\beta\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{(k)}\|_{M}^{2}}{4T}-\log{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{(k)}).

In the normalizing term, we empirically propose to replace the term ‖𝐱i(k)−𝐱j(k)‖M2\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{(k)}\|_{M}^{2} with a jj- and kk-dependent scaling ‖𝐱i(k)−𝐱j(k)‖Mj(k)2\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{(k)}\|_{M_{j}^{(k)}}^{2}. Using Laplace’s approximation, we have

𝒵⁡(𝐱j,Mj)\displaystyle{\mathcal{Z}}({\mathbf{x}}_{j};M_{j}) =∫ℝdexp⁡(−β2​(V​(z)+‖z−𝐱j‖Mj22​T))​dz\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\exp({-\frac{\beta}{2}(V(z) + \frac{\|z - \rvx_j\|_{M_j}^2}{2T})} )\differential{z} (49)
≈C⁡(β,T)​det⁡Mj​exp⁡(−β2​V​(𝐱j)).\displaystyle\approx C(\beta,T)\sqrt{\det M_{j}}\exp(-\frac{\beta}{2} V(\rvx_j)). (50)

Simplifying, the variable-preconditioner version of PBRWP takes the following form:

𝑿(k+1)=𝑿(k)−η2𝑴(k)∇V(𝑿(k))+η2​T(𝑿(k)−𝑿(k)softmax(W(k))⊤),\displaystyle{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k+1)}={\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)}-\frac{\eta}{2}{\bm{\mathsfit{M}}}^{(k)}\nabla V({\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)})+\frac{\eta}{2T}\left({\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)}-{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)}\mathrm{softmax}(W^{(k)})^{\top}\right), (51)
Wi,j(k)=−β​‖𝐱i(k)−𝐱j(k)‖Mj(k)24​T−12​log⁡det⁡(Mj(k))+β2​V​(𝐱j),\displaystyle W_{i,j}^{(k)}=-\beta\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{(k)}-{\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{(k)}\|_{M_{j}^{(k)}}^{2}}{4T}-\frac{1}{2}\log\det(M_j^{(k)})+\frac{\beta}{2}V({\mathbf{x}}_{j}), (52)

where 𝑴(k)∇V(𝑿(k))≔[M(k)1∇V(𝐱1)...MN(k)∇V(𝐱N)]{\bm{\mathsfit{M}}}^{(k)}\nabla V({\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(k)})\coloneqq\begin{bmatrix}M^{(k)}_{1}\nabla V({\mathbf{x}}_{1})&...&M_{N}^{(k)}\nabla V({\mathbf{x}}_{N})\end{bmatrix}.

For a neural network, the choice of preconditioner is a-priori unclear. For our experiments, we choose the diagonal preconditioner corresponding to the Adam optimizer [24], with exact implementation given in E. This has recently been linked to a diagonal approximation to the empirical Fisher information matrix [27, 22]. The diagonal form of the preconditioning matrix in this case makes it particularly amenable for the log-determinant in eq. 52.

To test, we train neural networks on various regression datasets, with N=10N=10 particles as in [45, 50]. The potential VV is given by the mean-squared error on the training dataset. Table 2 shows the root-mean-square error of the trained networks using PBRWP against various baselines. For the Adam baseline [24], we directly train from the initializations, where the step-size is chosen with a grid search to minimize the test RMSE. We observe that PBRWP is able to uniformly outperform BRWP on such a task, and is more competitive with kernel-based methods. This is analogous to Adam being empirically better than SGD for training neural networks.

7 Conclusion

This work proposes the Preconditioned Backwards Regularized Wasserstein Proximal (PBRWP) method Algorithm 1, a method of sampling without Langevin noise. Deriving the Cole–Hopf transform from a pair of anisotropic forward-backward heat equations, we obtain a coupled forward-time Fokker–Planck equation and backward-time Hamilton–Jacobi equation, both regularized with (elliptic) second-order differential operators. By applying a similar semi-implicit discretization to [45], we obtain particle swarm dynamics, interpretable as a self-attention mechanism. A discrete-time non-asymptotic convergence analysis is given in the case of quadratic potentials. Experiments demonstrate faster convergence with slightly more empirical bias, consistent with preconditioned Langevin methods.

While a fixed preconditioner MM has be shown to provide acceleration for some simple variational problems, the experiments in Section 6.7 empirically demonstrate that it is also possible to have variable preconditioners, such as that approximating the empirical Fisher information matrix. Future work would consider rigorous justification of variable preconditioners M=M⁡(x)M=M(x), such as those arising from inhomogeneous heat equations, or from Bregman divergences, similarly to mirror descent methods. Given that the PBRWP may be considered as a self-attention framework, future work may consider the converse implication. Additional theoretical analysis is also important. One part is the continuous-time convergence of the modified Fokker–Planck type equation eq. 30, which is not amenable to standard energy methods due to the variable kernel. The other is the discretization error from working with finitely many particles. While this arises from central limit and ergodicity results for standard Langevin methods, the final iteration approximation to the desired measure is less clear in the noiseless setting due to the per-particle convergence.

Proposition 12.

For a distribution ρk∼𝒩⁡(μk,Σk)\rho_{k}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(\mu_{k},\Sigma_{k}), the Wasserstein proximal satisfies WProxT,VM​ρk∼𝒩⁡(μ~k,Σ~k)\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\rho_{k}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(\tilde{\mu}_{k},\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}), where

Manipulating yields the desired expressions for μ~k\tilde{\mu}_{k} and Σ~k\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}.

B.3 Proof of discrete time convergence for Gaussians

Here we prove Theorem 10. We restate it here for convenience.

Theorem 13.

Suppose V⁡(x)=x⊤​Σ−1​x/2V(x)=x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x/2, and fix a β>0\beta>0. For the target distribution π=𝒩⁡(0,β−1​Σ)\pi={\mathcal{N}}(0,\beta^{-1}\Sigma) and positive definite preconditioner MM, let c,C>0c,C>0 be such that c​M⪯Σ⪯C​McM\preceq\Sigma\preceq CM. Let T∈(0,c)T\in(0,c) so that the inverse PRWPO is well-defined. Then there exists a stationary distribution to the discrete-time PBRWP iterations, and it is Gaussian π^=𝒩⁡(0,Σ^)\hat{\pi}={\mathcal{N}}(0,\hat{\Sigma}), satisfying WProxT,VM⁡(𝒩⁡(0,Σ^))=𝒩⁡(0,β−1​Σ)\wprox_{T,V}^{M}({\mathcal{N}}(0,\hat{\Sigma}))={\mathcal{N}}(0,\beta^{-1}\Sigma). Moreover, it is unique within distributions with sufficiently decaying Fourier transforms, specifically as given in Subsection C.1.

Suppose further that the initial Gaussian distribution ρ0=𝒩⁡(0,Σ0)\rho_{0}={\mathcal{N}}(0,\Sigma_{0}) has covariance commuting with Σ\Sigma, let ρk\rho_{k} be the iterations generated by PBRWP, and let ρ~k=WProxT,VM⁡(ρk)\tilde{\rho}_{k}=\wprox_{T,V}^{M}(\rho_{k}). Let λ\lambda be such that M−1​Σk​M−1\sqrt{M}^{-1}\Sigma_{k}\sqrt{M}^{-1} are uniformly bounded below by some λ\lambda (which holds as Σk→Σ\Sigma_{k}\rightarrow\Sigma). Let the step-size η\eta be bounded by

η​β−1≤min⁡((maxi⁡|λi​(Ξ~k−1−Ξ~∞−1)|)−1/2,3​λmin​(Ξ~k)/32)\eta\beta^{-1}\leq\min((\max_{i}|\lambda_{i}(\tilde{\Xi}_{k}^{-1}-\tilde{\Xi}_{\infty}^{-1})|)^{-1}/2,3\lambda_{\min}(\tilde{\Xi}_{k})/32)

then the exact discrete-time PBRWP method has the following decay in KL divergence:

DKL(ρ~k+1∥π)−DKL(ρ~k∥π)≤−η2​C​[β+2​T​(1+T​C−1)−1​(1+T​c−1)2​λ−1]DKL(ρ~k∥π).\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\tilde{\rho}_{k+1}\|\pi)-\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\tilde{\rho}_{k}\|\pi)\\ \leq-\frac{\eta}{2C[\beta+2T(1+TC^{-1})^{-1}(1+Tc^{-1})^{2}\lambda^{-1}]}\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\tilde{\rho}_{k}\|\pi). Proof.

We show convergence rates and existence first. Σk+1=(I−η​M​Σ−1+η​β−1​M​Σ~k−1)​Σk​(I−η​M​Σ−1+η​β−1​M​Σ~k−1)⊤.\Sigma_{k+1}=(I-\eta M\Sigma^{-1}+\eta\beta^{-1}M\tilde{\Sigma}^{-1}_{k})\Sigma_{k}(I-\eta M\Sigma^{-1}+\eta\beta^{-1}M\tilde{\Sigma}^{-1}_{k})^{\top}. (67)

Uniqueness: now we have established existence of a stationary solution as the Gaussian 𝒩⁡(0,Σ∞){\mathcal{N}}(0,\Sigma_{\infty}) satisfying WProxT,VM⁡(𝒩⁡(0,Σ∞))=𝒩⁡(0,β−1​Σ)\wprox_{T,V}^{M}({\mathcal{N}}(0,\Sigma_{\infty}))={\mathcal{N}}(0,\beta^{-1}\Sigma). From the modified Fokker–Planck equation (30), stationarity at a distribution ν\nu is equivalent to satisfying WProxT,VM​ν∝exp⁡(−β​V)=𝒩⁡(0,β−1​Σ)\wprox_{T,V}^{M}\nu\propto\exp(-\beta V)={\mathcal{N}}(0,\beta^{-1}\Sigma). Consider the definition of the regularized Wasserstein proximal as the coupled Fokker–Planck and Hamilton–Jacobi equation, plus the Cole–Hopf transformation. Since the forward- and backwards- anisotropic heat equations are well defined and are injective, the inverse of the Wasserstein proximal is unique.

Appendix C Additional results

C.1 Sufficient conditions for a unique inverse proximal

We wish to find sufficient conditions on a distribution ρ\rho such that the PRWPO (20) is invertible, that is, there exists a unique distribution ρ0\rho_{0} for which ρ=WProxT,VM​ρ0\rho=\wprox_{T,V}^{M}\rho_{0} is the preconditioned regularized Wasserstein proximal. Equivalently, from (14), we find sufficient conditions that the backward heat equation for η^\hat{\eta} from time TT to 0 is well defined. The forward heat equation is always well defined.

Recall that the solution to the anisotropic (forward) heat equation

∂tf=β−1∇⋅(M∇f)\partial_{t}f=\beta^{-1}\nabla\cdot(M\nabla f)

is given in Fourier space by

f⁡(t,x)=∫ℝdf^​(ξ)​ei⁡⟨ξ,x⟩−t​β−1​ξ⊤​M​ξ​dξ.f(t,x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\hat{f}(\xi)e^{i\langle\xi,x\rangle-t\beta^{-1}\xi^{\top}M\xi}\differential\xi. (84)

In order for f⁡(−T,x)f(-T,x) to be well defined by Plancherel’s theorem, we simply need that the Fourier transform f^​(ξ)\hat{f}(\xi) decays faster than e−T​β−1​ξ⊤​M​ξe^{-T\beta^{-1}\xi^{\top}M\xi}. Since the terminal condition for η^\hat{\eta} is η^(T,x)=ρ(x)e−βΦ(T,M−1x)/2=ρ(T,x)eβ​V​(x)/2\hat{\eta}(T,x)=\rho(x)e^{-\beta\Phi(T,M^{-1}x)/2}=\rho(T,x)e^{\beta V(x)/2}, which evolves through the backward heat equation, we want ρ⁡(x)​eβ​V​(x)/2\rho(x)e^{\beta V(x)/2} to have Fourier transform decaying (at least) faster than e−T​β−1​ξ⊤​M​ξe^{-T\beta^{-1}\xi^{\top}M\xi}.

C.1.1 Application: maximum value of T

Consider the quadratic potential case where V=x⊤​Σ−1​x/2V=x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x/2, and we wish to find ρ0\rho_{0} whose regularized Wasserstein proximal is proportional to exp⁡(−β​V)\exp(-\beta V). The Fourier transform of a normal distribution ρ∼𝒩⁡(μ,Σ)\rho\sim{\mathcal{N}}(\mu,\Sigma) (up to some factors of 2​π\sqrt{2\pi}) is

ρ^=𝔼x∼ρ​[e−i​⟨ξ,x⟩]=ei⁡⟨ξ,μ⟩−12​ξ⊤​Σ​ξ.\hat{\rho}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}\left[e^{-i\langle\xi,x\rangle}\right]=e^{i\langle\xi,\mu\rangle-\frac{1}{2}\xi^{\top}\Sigma\xi}. (85)

In this case, ρ​exp⁡(β​V/2)∝exp(−βV/2)\rho\exp(\beta V/2)\propto\exp(-\beta V/2) is proportional to a Gaussian with covariance 2​β−1​Σ2\beta^{-1}\Sigma, and thus the decay of the Fourier transform is ∼e−β−1​ξ⊤​Σ​ξ\sim e^{-\beta^{-1}\xi^{\top}\Sigma\xi}. This is at least faster than e−T​β−1​ξ⊤​M​ξe^{-T\beta^{-1}\xi^{\top}M\xi} if and only if Σ⪰T​M\Sigma\succeq TM.

C.2 Regularized Wasserstein proximal is a Wasserstein-2 contraction

From (36) or eq. 64, we have that KMK_{M} is a composition of the Gaussian convolution Markov kernel δy↦𝒩⁡(y,(β​Σ−12+β​M−12​T)−1)\delta_{y}\mapsto{\mathcal{N}}(y,(\frac{\beta\Sigma^{-1}}{2}+\frac{\beta M^{-1}}{2T})^{-1}) with the (linear) map ω:ℝd→ℝd\omega:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}, defined as y↦(Σ−12+M−12​T)−1​M−12​T​yy\mapsto(\frac{\Sigma^{-1}}{2}+\frac{M^{-1}}{2T})^{-1}\frac{M^{-1}}{2T}y. Since c−1​M−1⪰Σ−1⪰C−1​M−1c^{-1}M^{-1}\succeq\Sigma^{-1}\succeq C^{-1}M^{-1}, we have that β​Σ−12+β​M−12​T⪰(β​C−12+β2​T)​M−1\frac{\beta\Sigma^{-1}}{2}+\frac{\beta M^{-1}}{2T}\succeq(\frac{\beta C^{-1}}{2}+\frac{\beta}{2T})M^{-1}. Therefore the eigenvalues of the scaling matrix satisfy

λi​(M−12​T​(Σ−12+M−12​T)−2​M−12​T)≤(C−12+12​T)−2​(12​T)2<1.\lambda_{i}\left(\frac{M^{-1}}{2T}\left(\frac{\Sigma^{-1}}{2}+\frac{M^{-1}}{2T}\right)^{-2}\frac{M^{-1}}{2T}\right)\\ \leq\left(\frac{C^{-1}}{2}+\frac{1}{2T}\right)^{-2}\left(\frac{1}{2T}\right)^{2}<1.

In particular, the scaling map ω\omega is contractive with constant ζ≔(C−12+12​T)−1​(12​T)<1\zeta\coloneqq(\frac{C^{-1}}{2}+\frac{1}{2T})^{-1}(\frac{1}{2T})<1.

Let μ,ν∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu,\nu\in{\mathcal{P}}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be any probability measures with finite second moment, and let γ∈Π⁡(μ,ν)\gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu). We wish to bound

𝒲2​(WProxT,VM​μ,WProxT,VM​ν).{\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\mu,\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\nu).

Note that WProxT,VM​μ=𝒩⁡(0,(β​Σ−12+β​M−12​T)−1)∗ω#​μ\wprox^{M}_{T,V}\mu={\mathcal{N}}(0,(\frac{\beta\Sigma^{-1}}{2}+\frac{\beta M^{-1}}{2T})^{-1})*\omega_{\#}\mu. Since ω\omega is a contractive map with constant ζ\zeta, we have that

𝒲2​(𝒩⁡(0,(β​Σ−12+β​M−12​T)−1)∗μ,𝒩⁡(0,(β​Σ−12+β​M−12​T)−1)∗ν)≤𝒲2​(μ,ν).{\mathcal{W}}_{2}\left({\mathcal{N}}\left(0,\left(\frac{\beta\Sigma^{-1}}{2}+\frac{\beta M^{-1}}{2T}\right)^{-1}\right)*\mu,{\mathcal{N}}\left(0,\left(\frac{\beta\Sigma^{-1}}{2}+\frac{\beta M^{-1}}{2T}\right)^{-1}\right)*\nu\right)\leq{\mathcal{W}}_{2}(\mu,\nu). C.3 Mean reversion from high variance initialization

We list some simple definitions and properties before stating the inequality proposition 18. We fix β=1\beta=1 for simplicity.

Definition 15 (Relative Smoothness/Convexity).

Let Ψ:𝒳→ℝ\Psi:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a differentiable convex function, defined on a convex set 𝒳\mathcal{X} (with non-empty interior), which will be used as a reference. Let f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be another differentiable convex function.

ff is LL-smooth relative to Ψ\Psi if for any x,y∈int​(𝒳)x,y\in\text{int}(\mathcal{X}),

f⁡(y)≤f⁡(x)+⟨∇f​(x),y−x⟩+L​BΨ​(y,x).f(y)\leq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+LB_{\Psi}(y,x). (89)

ff is μ\mu-strongly-convex relative to Ψ\Psi if for any x,y∈int​(𝒳)x,y\in\text{int}(\mathcal{X}),

f⁡(y)≥f⁡(x)+⟨∇f​(x),y−x⟩+μ​BΨ​(y,x).f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\mu B_{\Psi}(y,x). (90)

In the special case where Ψ⁡(x)=12​x⊤​A​x\Psi(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax for some (positive definite) symmetric AA, we write that ff is LL-smooth relative to AA and μ\mu-strongly-convex relative to AA respectively. In particular, we have that BΨ​(x,y)=12​(x−y)⊤​A​(x−y)B_{\Psi}(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}(x-y)^{\top}A(x-y).

Proposition 16 (Control on spectral radius).

For a row- (or column-) stochastic matrix A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, the spectral norm ‖A‖2\|A\|_{2} equals its largest singular value σ1​(A)\sigma_{1}(A), and moreover satisfies ‖A‖2≤n\|A\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{n}.

Proof.

‖A‖2≤n​‖A‖∞=n\|A\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{n}\|A\|_{\infty}=\sqrt{n}, where ∥⋅∥∞\|\cdot\|_{\infty} is the induced ∞\infty-norm, equal to the maximum absolute row sum.

Proposition 17.

A function f:ℝn→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is μ\mu-strongly convex relative to AA if and only if for all x,y∈ℝnx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

⟨∇f​(x)−∇f​(y),x−y⟩≥μ⁡⟨A⁡(x−y),x−y⟩.\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\geq\mu\langle A(x-y),x-y\rangle. (91)

Proof.

Note that μ\mu-relative strong convexity is equivalent to f−μ​Ψf-\mu\Psi being convex. Hence, ff being μ\mu-strongly convex relative to 12​x⊤​A​x\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax is equivalent to the following by the monotone gradient condition,

⟨∇(f−μ​Ψ)​(x)−∇(f−μ​Ψ)​(y),x−y⟩≥0.\langle\nabla(f-\mu\Psi)(x)-\nabla(f-\mu\Psi)(y),x-y\rangle\geq 0.
⇔⟨∇f​(x)−∇f​(y),x−y⟩≥μ⁡⟨∇Ψ​(x)−∇Ψ​(y),x−y⟩=μ⁡⟨A⁡(x−y),x−y⟩.\Leftrightarrow\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\geq\mu\langle\nabla\Psi(x)-\nabla\Psi(y),x-y\rangle=\mu\langle A(x-y),x-y\rangle.

Appendix D Sensitivity to hyperparameters for imaging experiment

Tables 3 and 4 plot the deconvolution reconstructions using PBRWP and BRWP respectively over a variety of choices of TT and step-size. Both methods are run with 40 particles up to 5000 iterations. We observe that both methods are not particularly sensitive to the choice of TT except for an intermediate choice of T=10−2T=10^{-2}, for which we observe more variance. This can be explained by variance reduction phenomena: by the regularization of the Wasserstein proximal for large TT, and by the finite number of particles for small TT. For the smallest step-size η=10−5\eta=10^{-5}, 5000 iterations are insufficient to reach convergence and therefore the performance is worse.

Appendix E Choice of variable preconditioner for BNNs

To compute the diagonal variable preconditioner, we use the second moment estimates of Adam [24], which are used to precondition a moving average of the gradient. We discard the first moment estimate since we are not optimizing using Adam directly. Algorithm 2 details how pointwise gradient estimates (corresponding to each particle) give rise to the variable preconditioning matrices M(k)M^{(k)}. By applying this algorithm to each particle 𝐱j{\mathbf{x}}_{j}, which are updated according to PBRWP, we get their corresponding preconditioning matrices Mj(k)M^{(k)}_{j}.
